# Host (pacman) packages that must be PRESENT for this config to work.
# system/deploy converges pacman onto this file on every run, on the hosts its
# own allow-list names, so a line added here reaches setsuna/utsuho/shiori on
# their next `mise run system:deploy` -- which is the point. pacstrap's list only
# ever reached the *next* new box, which is how fprintd stayed uninstalled for
# months after being wired up in hyprlock and pam.d.
#
# What belongs here: things that must be root-side, because a user profile
# cannot provide them -- a system systemd unit, a system D-Bus service, a module
# the host's own libraries dlopen by name, firmware, state under /var. Anything
# a user can own belongs in home.nix.
#
# What does NOT belong here, and lives in install/packages-install-only instead:
# anything only a *fresh install* needs. The kernel especially -- enforcing
# `linux` would install a second, stock kernel on a host running linux-lts or
# -zen -- and the shell tools install-base.sh needs before home-manager exists.
# That file is pacstrapped once and never enforced again.
#
# Hardware packages sort by whether being wrong is harmful or merely inert:
# intel-ucode and the Intel video drivers are picked per host and stay inline in
# install-base.sh, because pushing them at the AMD boxes would be wrong; fprintd
# and sof-firmware sit here, because a box without the hardware just never
# exercises them.
#
# Format: one package per line, # comments, blank lines ignored. Package names
# only -- `pacman -Qq` resolves virtual provides (`sh` answers bash) but NOT
# groups, so a group line would read as missing on every single deploy.

# disks: the encrypted btrfs root and the ESP
btrfs-progs
cryptsetup
dosfstools

# network and remote access
networkmanager
openssh
sudo

# The account's login shell is the absolute path /bin/zsh (install-base.sh's
# useradd -s), which no nix profile can provide -- home.nix owns zsh's
# configuration, not that path. So the binary is a host package.
zsh

# graphics
mesa

# audio
sof-firmware
pipewire
pipewire-pulse
pipewire-alsa
wireplumber

# firmware blobs for the kernel, whichever kernel that is
linux-firmware

# system services
polkit
tpm2-tss
tpm2-tools
bluez
bluez-utils
fwupd
power-profiles-daemon

# Fingerprint reader (Goodix 27c6:609c on shiori). Cannot come from nix: the
# host's PAM dlopens pam_fprintd.so by bare name out of /usr/lib/security (see
# etc/pam.d/polkit-1), fprintd itself is a root-run system D-Bus service, and
# its enrollments are root state in /var/lib/fprint. hyprlock's
# fingerprint.enabled (home.nix) reaches the daemon over D-Bus rather than PAM,
# so it silently no-ops when the package is absent.
# Enrolling stays manual and per-host: `fprintd-enroll`, then `fprintd-list`.

# Linux Support for Framework Laptop 13 Pro (Intel Core Ultra Series 3, 2026)

## Ubuntu Certification & Official Support

The device is **Framework's first Ubuntu Certified system**, certified against **Ubuntu 24.04 LTS**. Framework pre-loads **Ubuntu 26.04 LTS** on Ubuntu models and officially supports:
- Ubuntu 26.04 LTS
- Fedora 44

Community-supported distributions include CachyOS, Bazzite, Arch, and NixOS 26.05.

## Kernel Requirements

- **Minimum:** Kernel 6.19
- **Wi-Fi 7 (BE211):** Requires kernel ≥6.9

Per Phoronix testing, "Ubuntu 26.04 LTS worked great out-of-the-box on kernel 7.0."

## Known Issues & Caveats

**USB-C Charger Compatibility (Linux)**
Phoronix discovered that using a third-party 150W Anker charger capped the Core Ultra X9's power draw at 6W, drastically reducing performance. The included Framework charger resolved this—a unique issue not seen on prior Framework models.

**Thermals**
Single-fan cooling is the limiting factor; Notebookcheck measured CPU temperatures exceeding 90°C under load (versus 74°C on competing Dell XPS 13 with the same chip).

## Resources

An official **Ubuntu 26.04 LTS installation guide** is published at Framework's support site. The wiki does not detail specific suspend, power management, graphics driver, fingerprint, audio, or fwupd configurations for this model.

# Framework's Linux Support for Laptop 13 Pro

## Supported Distros
Framework officially supports:
- **Fedora 44** (Intel Core Ultra Series 3 & AMD Ryzen AI 300)
- **Ubuntu 26.04** (both processor variants)
- **Ubuntu 24.04 LTS** (pre-built OEM edition)

Community-supported options include CachyOS, Bazzite, Arch Linux, and NixOS 26.05.

## Kernel Requirements
"Minimum: 6.19 | Recommended: 7.0+ | Best Experience: Latest"

## Design Philosophy
Framework states the Laptop 13 Pro is "designed and tested for Linux compatibility from the ground up." The company validates hardware across major distributions, contributes upstream when possible, and provides firmware integrated through LVFS. Component selection prioritizes Linux compatibility for Wi-Fi, fingerprint readers, audio, and power management.

## Known Support Levels
Officially supported distros feature:
- Wi-Fi and Bluetooth working out of the box
- Fingerprint reader functionality
- Stable operation with easy setup

Community-supported options may require additional configuration for certain features, particularly fingerprint reader setup on Arch Linux and NixOS.

Beta firmware builds can sometimes be found on the testing remote [https://community.frame.work/t/bios-3-09-beta-release/20085#lvfs-update-6], which can be enabled by running: $ fwupdmgr enable-remote lvfs-testing {{Note| * As of August 2025, only the original 11th Gen Intel mainboards lack any stable BIOS updates on LVFS, partly due to the mandatory Intel CSME patches in BIOS updates newer than 3.17. You should not enable the testing remote on newer mainboards if you want to use only stable BIOS updates and not those in beta testing [https://knowledgebase.frame.work/framework-laptop-bios-and-driver-releases-amd-ryzen-7040-series-r1rXGVL16][https://knowledgebase.frame.work/en_us/updating-bios-on-linux-Hk4pROTn]. * 11th Gen Intel Mainboards with BIOS versions earlier than 3.17 only have in-memory capsule update support, not on-disk. To upgrade to newer versions with the support, add the following fwupd configuration changes, update to 3.17 or higher, and then revert the change after the BIOS is updated: {{hc|/etc/fwupd/fwupd.conf|2= [uefi_capsule] DisableCapsuleUpdateOnDisk=true }} }} ==== Fingerprint reader ==== Framework has [https://knowledgebase.frame.work/en_us/updating-fingerprint-reader-firmware-on-linux-for-13th-gen-and-amd-ryzen-7040-series-laptops-HJrvxv_za published a guide] for Intel 13th Gen and AMD to upgrade the firmware to a known working version. === Secure Boot === {{Expansion|Add links to official sources or forum posts for each model that can be enrolled with custom keys.|section=Custom Secure Boot keys}} One can enroll custom keys into the Framework Laptop without any Option ROM concerns, or use the SHIM approach. See [[Secure Boot]] for details. === Suspend === On Intel boards, adding the [[kernel parameter]] {{ic|1=acpi_osi="!Windows 2020"}} fixes a regression in s2idle, making the keyboard backlight and power button correctly turn off when suspending, as well as decreasing battery drain in suspend to about 1%/hour[https://community.frame.work/t/solved-laptop-stays-on-in-sleep/17168]. If your system fails to wake up from suspend due to the SSD disconnecting, you can try putting {{ic|1=nvme.noacpi=1}} in your [[kernel parameters]]. This may also improve battery life in suspend, if your SSD has a bad ACPI implementation. This should only be used on Intel boards, as on AMD it will cause the issue, instead of fixing it. {{Warning|Some NVMe drives do not successfully wake from the deep sleep state described below, disconnecting from the laptop and becoming inaccessible until a reboot, which typically causes the laptop to lock up. One example is the Sabrent Rocket NVMe 4.0[https://community.frame.work/t/linux-deep-sleep/2491/48][https://community.frame.work/t/ubuntu-21-04-on-the-framework-laptop/2722/30]. Before enabling this sleep state in a production installation, you may wish to test the suspend functionality of your NVMe drive from the Arch installer environment so as not to cause corruption.}} See [[Power management/Suspend and hibernate#Changing suspend method]] if you want to use S3 sleep instead of s2idle. ==== Fn key after suspend ==== Some users on 11th-generation Intel boards report that after resuming from suspend, the Fn key and/or media keys no longer work. The workaround is to blacklist the {{ic|1=cros_ec_lpcs}} module: {{hc|/etc/modprobe.d/cros_ec_lpcs.conf|2= blacklist cros_ec_lpcs }} ==== Wakeup triggers ==== {{Warning|This section is solved by updating to the most recent BIOS version, this is only for legacy BIOS. [https://github.com/FrameworkComputer/linux-docs/blob/main/disable-accidental-wakeup/readme.md#disable-accidental-wakeup-script See Here]}} If your Framework wakes up while being transported in a backpack or bag, this is because of [https://community.frame.work/t/firmware-feature-request-disable-keypress-while-the-lid-is-closed/49464 the screen pressing against the keyboard]. Deactivating the keyboard [[Wakeup triggers|Wakeup trigger]] solves this. Deactivate until next reboot: # echo disabled > /sys/devices/platform/i8042/serio0/power/wakeup Deactivate starting next reboot: {{hc|/etc/udev/rules.d/disable-keyboard-wakeup.rules|2= ACTION=="add", SUBSYSTEM=="serio", DRIVERS=="atkbd", ATTR{power/wakeup}="disabled" }} Alternatively to disable both keypresses and touchpad is: # echo disabled > /sys/devices/platform/AMDI0010:03/i2c-1/i2c-PIXA3854:00/power/wakeup Framework [https://github.com/FrameworkComputer/linux-docs/blob/main/disable-accidental-wakeup/readme.md#disable-accidental-wakeup-script provides a script] which creates a systemd triger to set it up after reboots. Also see [https://community.frame.work/t/responded-waking-from-suspend-w-lid-closed/47497/95?u=adaschma their forum post] for more discussions. === Touchpad === There are reports of the touchpad exhibiting issues (e.g. pointer does not move, two-finger scroll does not work, etc.) after waking from sleep. Disabling PS/2 mouse emulation under Advanced in the BIOS seems to resolve the issues[https://community.frame.work/t/sleep-and-touchpad-not-responding/4928/16]. === Interact with system === You can interact with your system using {{Pkg|framework-system}}. On 11th and 12th Gen Intel boards, you can also interact with the embedded controller using {{AUR|fw-ectool-git}}. {{Warning|The Embedded Controller on your Framework Laptop handles low level functions, including power sequencing the system. Modifying the EC code can cause your system to not power on or boot or cause damage to the mainboard, battery, or other parts of the system or devices attached to the system. '''Hardware damage caused by EC firmware modifications would not be covered under the Framework Limited Warranty.'''}}

== Ambient light sensor ==

Should work out of the box, you can check by reading {{ic|1=/sys/bus/iio/devices/iio\:device0/in_illuminance_raw}}.

On [[KDE|Plasma]] (starting from version 6.6) and [[GNOME]], you need to install {{Pkg|iio-sensor-proxy}} and restart the session (or reboot, just in case). Then run {{ic|monitor-sensor}} to check if it is working.

If you do not use Plasma or GNOME but still want automatic brightness control, check out {{Pkg|illuminanced}}.

{{Note|This does not work if you have [[#12th gen Turbo-Boost on battery with tlp|blacklisted the {{ic|hid_sensor_hub}} module]].}}

== Fan speed control ==

You can force the fan speed to any value between 0 and 100 using this tool: https://gitlab.howett.net/DHowett/ectool ({{AUR|fw-ectool-git}})
 $ ectool --interface=lpc fanduty 1OO
to return to automatic mode use this command:
 $ ectool --interface=lpc autofanctrl

In the meantime: https://lore.kernel.org/chrome-platform/20231005160701.19987-1-dustin@howett.net/ for direct support of the EC chromium driver.

== Battery control ==

Framework laptops have an [https://community.frame.work/t/exploring-the-embedded-controller/12846 embedded controller] responsible for controlling a variety of functions (fans, battery, LEDs...). Settings for this EC can be changed with {{AUR|fw-ectool-git}} until patches are merged into the mainline kernel, or alternatively with the ''framework_tool'' binary in {{pkg|framework-system}}. [https://github.com/MrChromebox/firmware/issues/420 Some of the exposed settings related to battery health care] are:

 # ectool chargecontrol idle

 # ectool chargecontrol normal ''lower'' ''upper''

chargecontrol can be set to discharge, idle, and normal. Discharge makes the system use the energy from the battery, disabling the charger; normal allows setting lower and upper limits (the battery stays in discharge mode while the battery level is between the upper and lower limits, and starts charging when the level is below the lower limit); and idle allows the system to get all the energy from the charger, essentially leaving the battery unused and avoiding any wear. This is very useful for using the laptop as an always-plugged-in device. Setting lower = upper values automatically sets idle mode after reaching the target value, while using idle keeps the battery in idle mode at the current charge level.

You can check how much current is being withdrawn from or charged into the battery with:

 # cat /sys/class/power_supply/BAT0/current_now

Or under Present current in:

 # ectool battery

Using:

 # ectool fwchargelimit ''level''

seems to do the same as setting the charge limit through BIOS, which tries to maintain the battery level at the set level but is constantly charging and discharging it (no idle mode is used in this mode).

Finally, we can set a limit to the max current allowed for charging, thus enabling slow charging, with:

 # ectool chargecurrentlimit ''mA''

Parameters set via ectool remains active until the laptop is powered off and unplugged for a few (10~) seconds, after which values go back to default.

== Troubleshooting ==

=== Stuttering, flickering and periodic freeze ===

There are reports of stuttering, flickering and periodic freezes on the laptop. Disabling Panel Self-Refresh (as explained in [[Intel graphics#Screen flickering]]) has been [https://community.frame.work/t/periodic-stuttering-on-fresh-gnome-40-wayland-install-on-arch-linux/3912/6 reported to work]. However it is helpful for battery life, so it should be left on if there are no issues.

This [https://www.reddit.com/r/archlinux/comments/11geaq4/framework_laptop_12th_gen_intel_igpu_flickering/ can also happen] if you have installed {{Pkg|xf86-video-intel}} instead of using modesetting, see the note at [[Intel graphics#Installation]].

=== Two/three finger clicks ===

By default, the touchpad provides middle and right click by clicking on specific regions (bottom middle for middle click and bottom right corner for right click). To switch this two-finger click for right click and three-finger click for middle click, you will need to set the "click method" via [[libinput]]. First, find your "Touchpad" device name:

 $ xinput

And then set the click method, where {{ic|''device''}} is the name (or ID) found in the previous step:

 $ xinput set-prop "''device''" "libinput Click Method Enabled" 0 1

To make this persistent, put it in a startup script. Alternatively, if using X11, one can create a custom Xorg configuration file with the appropriate settings (see [[libinput#Via Xorg configuration file]]).

=== HiDPI settings ===

* For the 2256x1504 display using scaling factor 1,5 is suggested.
* For the 2880x1920 (2.8K) display using scaling factor 2 is suggested.

For more details, see [[HiDPI]].

=== Lowering fan noise ===

'''This applies to the Intel version only. AMD users should use power-profiles-daemon.'''

The handling of fans can be significantly improved by using the {{Pkg|thermald}} service. Install the package and then you can [[Start]] and [[Enable]] the service via the {{ic|thermald.service}} unit file.

=== Changing the brightness of the monitor does not work ===

See [[Backlight#xbacklight returns : No outputs have backlight property]].

For Alder Lake CPUs a solution for using the backlight keys instead of the light sensor is to deactivate the ambient light sensor.
{{hc
|/etc/modprobe.d/framework-als-deactivate.conf|
blacklist hid_sensor_hub
}}

Reboot is required, the light sensor module will be deactivated and the backlight keys work.

Note that some minimal WMs/compositors, such as sway, do not automatically bind the brightness keys, so if you can adjust the brightness through other means but the fn keys do not work, that is likely to be the issue.

=== Bootmanager flashing black screen and not loading operating system ===

If your Framework laptop loads the [[boot loader]] and can recognize the [[EFI system partition]] on your flash drive or m.2. drive, but cannot load your boot manager (it only flashes a black screen before returning to the boot loader), you must disable [[Secure Boot]].

# Reboot holding {{ic|F2}}. There is a bug in some versions of the BIOS that prevents the {{ic|F2}} key on the builtin laptop keyboard from being recognized during reboot or power up. The workaround is to connect an external USB keyboard to the laptop an hold the {{ic|F2}} key on the external keyboard while rebooting or powering up the laptop. After the laptop has entered the BIOS settings the builtin keyboard can be used and the external one can be disconnected.

Do not edit files in `/home/sauyon/devel/dotfiles` directly on `master`. Branch
and work in a worktree, then merge. The user caught me mid-task editing the main
tree and said so bluntly ("why the fuck are you working in the main tree"),

**Why:** master is the tree `hms` reads, and `hms` refuses on a dirty tree — so
uncommitted edits in the main checkout block applying config, and they sit in the
one place the user expects to be clean. A worktree also keeps the main checkout
usable while work is in progress.

**How to apply:** `git worktree add .drovr/wt/<name> -b <branch> HEAD`, add
`.drovr/wt` to `.git/info/exclude` (not the tracked `.gitignore`), then
`EnterWorktree` into it. Note that master may be **amended** under you while you
work — check `git merge-base --is-ancestor <base> master` before merging, and
replay with `git rebase --onto master <base> <branch>` rather than a plain merge
that would resurrect rewritten commits.

Never treat `git push` as a step that can stand alone in this repo. If the
change is going to origin, run `hms` — it pushes, waits for the commit's CI run
on `forge.ko.ag`, then switches to the closure CI built. Offering "want me to
push?" as separate from switching was the mistake; the user's words: "god damn
if you push you MUST hms".

**Why:** a pushed-but-not-switched master is a half-applied state. CI builds
every pushed commit, so a push already commits the machine to that closure;
stopping before the switch just leaves the box running old config while origin
says otherwise, and the next `hms` then switches to a commit nobody reviewed as
current.

**How to apply:** when work is committed and ready, run `hms` (background it —
it blocks ten-odd minutes). Never propose `git push` on its own, and never
substitute `home-manager switch`. `hms --local` builds here instead of
downloading CI's build, and is a deliberate choice to state out loud.

When a change is verified by a harness, the harness belongs in `tests/` in the
commit, not in the session's scratch directory. Asked on 2026-09-27 whether to
commit one (and whether to apply with `hms`), the answer was "always do it" —

comments asserting the model is right are exactly what needs re-checking after an
upstream bump.

evaluates and realises the real artifact and tests that, so it runs with no
setup; a path argument tests a given build. Drive the code through override seams
(env vars) so no real failure state has to be provoked. Mention it in README.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Run as your normal user (e.g. `mise run deploy`), NOT under sudo: the sops
# steps below decrypt with your GCP key under $HOME and each privileged install
# sudo's itself. Running the whole script as root points $HOME at /root, so sops
# can't find the key (and root has no KMS creds) -- fail fast instead.
if [ "$(id -u)" -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "system/deploy: run as your user (try 'mise run system:deploy'), not root." >&2
  exit 1
fi

cd "$(dirname "$0")"

# ── host packages: converge pacman onto ./packages ───────────────────────────
# install-base.sh pacstraps the same list, but that only ever runs on the live
# ISO, so a package added after a host was built never reaches it.
#
# The order against the etc/ copy below does not matter, and it is worth saying
# so rather than inventing a reason: pacman owns NONE of the seven files that
# copy writes (`pacman -Qo` on each answers "No package owns"). Everything under
# etc/ is an override path -- /etc/pam.d/polkit-1 shadows the polkit package's
# /usr/lib/pam.d/polkit-1, /etc/systemd/system/tailscaled.service shadows the
# packaged unit -- which is the mechanism that makes this whole directory work.
# Nor does the order spare any pam_fprintd load errors: every existing host has
# had that state since the polkit-1 stack was committed, and a fresh host
# pacstraps fprintd before deploy ever runs.
#
# An explicit host list, NOT `command -v pacman`: those are different
# predicates. kyuusaku is a box whose OS we do not own, and an Arch-based one
# would sail through a capability check and be handed a base metapackage.
# docs/new-host.md step 0 says to add a new host here. It happens to be the same
# four hosts as home.nix's `hms` case, but for an unrelated reason (that one
# means "has a Linux CI job"), so do not treat the two as one list -- kyuusaku
# is absent from both for different reasons, and a CI job would earn it a place
# in hms without earning one here.
#
# A host that is not listed still gets the etc/ copy below, so it keeps a
# pam_fprintd line it cannot load -- fail-safe (polkit falls through to the
# password) at the price of a log line per auth.
#
# A failure here WARNS and carries on rather than aborting: nothing later in
# this script is about packages, and the attic netrc further down is what lets
# the home-manager switch after it download CI's closure instead of compiling
# for an hour. Letting a stale mirror take that down would be a worse outcome
# than a host missing fprintd. SKIP_HOST_PACKAGES to any value skips the step
# outright -- tested for non-emptiness, so SKIP_HOST_PACKAGES=0 skips too.
#
# Without --noconfirm this step can PROMPT (pacman's "Proceed with installation?"),
# so a deploy driven over ssh wants a tty. Without one, pacman takes its defaults
# or aborts, and either way the warn-and-continue above keeps the rest running.
#
# `uname -n`, not $HOSTNAME and not hostname(1): the kernel owns it where an env
# var is inheritable, the repo derives the host this way in three other places
# (home.nix's hms, two mise tasks), and hostname(1) lives in inetutils, which is
# installed on none of these boxes.
if [ -n "${SKIP_HOST_PACKAGES:-}" ]; then
  echo "system/deploy: SKIP_HOST_PACKAGES set -- not touching pacman."
else
host=$(uname -n)
case "${host%%.*}" in
utsuho | setsuna | shiori | fujiwara)
  [ -r packages ] || { echo "system/deploy: ./packages is missing or unreadable" >&2; exit 1; }
  # Strip comments, then split on any whitespace. One package per line is the
  # documented format; splitting rather than deleting whitespace means a
  # two-names-on-one-line slip fails as two packages instead of silently
  # concatenating into one bogus name.
  mapfile -t want < <(sed 's/#.*//' packages | tr -s '[:space:]' '\n' | sed '/^$/d')
  # mapfile returns 0 whatever the process substitution did, and neither `set
  # -e` nor pipefail sees inside one, so an empty parse has to be caught by
  # hand. Without this a renamed or emptied list makes this step a silent
  # no-op -- the exact failure the list was added to fix.
  [ ${#want[@]} -gt 0 ] || { echo "system/deploy: ./packages parsed to nothing" >&2; exit 1; }

  missing=()
  for p in "${want[@]}"; do
    # -Qq resolves virtual provides (`pacman -Qq sh` answers bash), so an entry
    # satisfied by a provider is not reported missing.
    pacman -Qq -- "$p" >/dev/null 2>&1 || missing+=("$p")
  done

  if [ ${#missing[@]} -gt 0 ]; then
    echo "system/deploy: installing missing host packages: ${missing[*]}"
    # `--` because the list is data: a line starting with a dash would
    # otherwise be read as a pacman option (--hookdir=, --overwrite=, --root=),
    # and this runs under sudo.
    #
    # No `--noconfirm`, which answers every question with its default -- and the
    # default to "replace X with Y?" is yes. So a line here that reads as purely
    # additive could silently REMOVE a package from a running host by pulling in
    # something that replaces it. (Whether the separate "X conflicts with Y,
    # remove Y?" question also defaults to yes I did not confirm; it does not
    # change the conclusion.) Prompting costs a keypress, and only when something
    # is actually missing.
    #
    # No `-y` either: refreshing the db and then installing without upgrading is
    # the partial-upgrade footgun. `-S` against the db as it stands resolves the
    # version matching the libraries already installed, which is the safe
    # direction. It is not a guarantee -- if the db is already newer than the
    # system because something ran `pacman -Sy` by hand, installing anything
    # here drags its newer deps in and you get a partial upgrade through the
    # other door. Nothing this script can do about that; `-Syu` is the cure.
    #
    # Failure is a warning, not an abort (see the header): a stale db 404, a
    # held pacman lock, a refused sudo password, a full /var, an unresolvable
    # conflict. Any of them, and the rest of the deploy still runs.
    sudo pacman -S --needed -- "${missing[@]}" || {
      echo "system/deploy: pacman failed for: ${missing[*]}" >&2
      echo "  Common causes: a stale sync db (404 on a dropped version -- fix" >&2
      echo "  with 'sudo pacman -Syu'), another pacman holding the db lock, or" >&2
      echo "  no network. Continuing; nothing below needs these packages." >&2
    }
  fi
  ;;
*)
  echo "system/deploy: ${host%%.*} is not one of our Arch hosts -- skipping host packages."
  ;;
esac
fi

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Install and enable thermald -- but only where it is the right answer, which is
# Intel and nowhere else.
#
# WHY IT IS NOT IN system/packages: that file is the list every host must have,
# and half of ours are AMD (utsuho, fujiwara; see flake.nix). thermald is an
# Intel-only daemon -- it drives the ACPI DPTF devices (int3400/int3403) and the
# processor_thermal_device RAPL/PL knobs, and on a non-Intel CPU it exits rather
# than running. Pushing it at the AMD boxes would be the same mistake as pushing
# intel-ucode at them, which is why those stay inline in install-base.sh's
# HW_PKGS. The packages file's own header draws this line: hardware packages
# sort by whether being wrong is harmful or merely inert, and a *service* that
# is wrong is never inert -- it is a failed unit on every boot.
#
# WHY IT IS NOT IN install-base.sh's `systemctl enable` line: that line runs once,
# inside the chroot, on a fresh install. shiori already exists. An enable that
# only ever reaches the next new host is exactly the drift the packages file was
# written to fix (fprintd stayed uninstalled for months that way), so this runs
# from system/deploy on every deploy instead.
#
# WHY thermald AT ALL: it is the Framework/Intel recommendation, not a hunch.
# ArchWiki's Framework Laptop 13 page ("Lowering fan noise") says fan handling is
# significantly improved by it and that it applies to the Intel version only;
# both distributions Framework certifies the Laptop 13 Pro against -- Ubuntu
# 26.04 LTS and Fedora 44 -- ship it by default on Intel; and Phoronix's Panther
# Lake power review ran its performance-profile numbers with thermald applied.
# shiori is a Framework Laptop 13 Pro (Core Ultra X7 358H, Panther Lake) and has
# the int3400/int3403 DPTF devices thermald steers.
#
# It coexists with power-profiles-daemon rather than replacing it: ppd sets the
# EPP and the ACPI platform_profile, thermald manages the passive trip points and
# fan response underneath. This is the pairing Fedora and Ubuntu both ship.
#
# Seams, for tests/thermald-setup.sh: CPUINFO overrides the vendor gate's source,
# and pacman/sudo/systemctl are resolved through PATH so the harness can stub
# them. Nothing here needs a real Intel host, a real package, or a real unit.
set -euo pipefail

cpuinfo=${CPUINFO:-/proc/cpuinfo}

# -s as well as -q: an unreadable or absent cpuinfo reads as "not Intel" and we
# skip, which is the safe direction. The failure mode of guessing wrong the
# other way is a failed unit on a box that can never run the daemon.
if ! grep -qs '^vendor_id[[:space:]]*:[[:space:]]*GenuineIntel' "$cpuinfo"; then
  echo "system/thermald-setup: not an Intel CPU -- skipping thermald."
  exit 0
fi

# Ask before acting, both here and below, so a converged host costs zero sudo
# prompts. `system/deploy` runs on every `mise run system:deploy`; a step that
# unconditionally sudo'd would train the password prompt into background noise.
if ! pacman -Qq thermald >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "system/thermald-setup: installing thermald"
  # Same flags and the same reasoning as the packages step in system/deploy:
  # `--` because the name is data, no --noconfirm (its default answer to
  # "replace X with Y?" is yes), and no -y (refresh-then-install without
  # upgrading is the partial-upgrade footgun).
  sudo pacman -S --needed -- thermald || {
    echo "system/thermald-setup: pacman failed for thermald; not enabling it." >&2
    exit 1
  }
fi

# `enable --now` is idempotent, but is-enabled/is-active are not privileged and
# `enable --now` is, so checking first is what keeps the no-op path prompt-free.
# Both halves matter: enabled-but-stopped is a real state (someone stopped it
# this boot), and started-but-disabled dies at the next reboot.
if [ "$(systemctl is-enabled thermald.service 2>/dev/null)" != enabled ] ||
  [ "$(systemctl is-active thermald.service 2>/dev/null)" != active ]; then
  echo "system/thermald-setup: enabling thermald.service"
  sudo systemctl enable --now thermald.service
fi

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Cases for system/thermald-setup, the Intel-only install-and-enable step
# system/deploy runs on every deploy. They drive the real script through its
# seams -- CPUINFO for the vendor gate, and stub pacman/sudo/systemctl on PATH --
# so no case needs an Intel host, a real thermald package, or a real unit, and
# none of them can touch the running system.
#
# What is actually being protected here: half our hosts are AMD (utsuho,
# fujiwara), and the cost of the gate being wrong is asymmetric. Too loose and
# two boxes carry a unit that fails on every boot; too tight and shiori quietly
# never gets the daemon that Framework's own certified distros ship. The other
# half of the cases are about the no-op path staying silent -- a converged host
# must cost zero sudo prompts, or the password prompt becomes background noise
# and the next deploy that really needs it gets waved through.
#
#   ./tests/thermald-setup.sh                 # tests system/thermald-setup
#   ./tests/thermald-setup.sh /path/to/script # tests one you already have
set -u

SCRIPT="${1:-$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../system" && pwd)/thermald-setup}"
[ -x "$SCRIPT" ] || { echo "not executable: $SCRIPT" >&2; exit 1; }
echo "testing $SCRIPT"

D=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$D"' EXIT
fails=0; n=0

# --- stubs -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Each records its argv in $D/calls and answers from a STUB_* variable, so a case
# is written as "what the host looks like" rather than as a script of mocks.
mkdir -p "$D/bin"

cat > "$D/bin/pacman" <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "pacman $*" >> "$CALLS"
case "$1" in
-Qq) exit "${STUB_INSTALLED:-1}" ;;   # 0 = thermald already installed
-S)  exit "${STUB_PACMAN_S:-0}" ;;
esac
exit 0
EOF

# Not `exec "$@"` blindly: recording the sudo itself is what lets a case assert
# that the converged path never escalates at all.
cat > "$D/bin/sudo" <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "sudo $*" >> "$CALLS"
exec "$@"
EOF

cat > "$D/bin/systemctl" <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "systemctl $*" >> "$CALLS"
case "$1" in
is-enabled) echo "${STUB_ENABLED:-disabled}"; [ "${STUB_ENABLED:-disabled}" = enabled ] ;;
is-active)  echo "${STUB_ACTIVE:-inactive}";  [ "${STUB_ACTIVE:-inactive}" = active ] ;;
enable)     exit "${STUB_ENABLE_RC:-0}" ;;
esac
exit 0
EOF

chmod +x "$D/bin"/*

printf 'vendor_id\t: GenuineIntel\nmodel name\t: Intel(R) Core(TM) Ultra X7 358H\n' > "$D/intel"
printf 'vendor_id\t: AuthenticAMD\nmodel name\t: AMD Ryzen 7 7840U\n' > "$D/amd"
: > "$D/empty"

# --- runner ------------------------------------------------------------------
# want_rc, then a list of "+needle" (must appear in the call log) and "-needle"
# (must not). Env for the case comes in as leading VAR=value arguments.
run_case() { # desc cpuinfo want_rc [VAR=val ...] [--] [+/-needle ...]
  local desc=$1 cpuinfo=$2 want_rc=$3; shift 3
  local env=() rc out
  while [ $# -gt 0 ] && [ "$1" != -- ]; do env+=("$1"); shift; done
  [ $# -gt 0 ] && shift

  n=$((n + 1))
  : > "$D/calls"
  out=$(env PATH="$D/bin:$PATH" CALLS="$D/calls" CPUINFO="$cpuinfo" \
    "${env[@]}" "$SCRIPT" 2>&1)
  rc=$?

  local bad=()
  [ "$rc" = "$want_rc" ] || bad+=("exit $rc, wanted $want_rc")
  local needle
  for needle in "$@"; do
    case "$needle" in
    +*) grep -qF -- "${needle#+}" "$D/calls" || bad+=("missing call: ${needle#+}") ;;
    -*) grep -qF -- "${needle#-}" "$D/calls" && bad+=("unwanted call: ${needle#-}") ;;
    esac
  done

  if [ ${#bad[@]} -eq 0 ]; then
    echo "ok   $desc"
  else
    fails=$((fails + 1))
    echo "FAIL $desc"
    printf '       %s\n' "${bad[@]}"
    printf '       calls: %s\n' "$(tr '\n' '; ' < "$D/calls")"
    [ -n "$out" ] && printf '       output: %s\n' "$out"
  fi
}

# --- the vendor gate ---------------------------------------------------------
# The whole point of the script. An AMD host must come out the far side having

Base directory for this skill: /nix/store/REDACTED/skills/code-review

# Code Review

## Overview

**They find, you fix.** Follow the spirit, not the letter: dispatching a
reviewer satisfies the letter; one that read an empty diff, or that you never
waited for, looked at nothing and found nothing. The rule is that
somebody who did not write the change has said what is wrong with it — and that
cannot be you. You read the change you meant to make, not the one on disk.

**Write for the agent who inherits this: the next phase agent is you, with your
context gone.** A finding you settled in your head is one they meet as a bug,
with nothing saying anyone saw it.

## The Iron Law

```
NO CHANGE IS DONE UNTIL A READ-ONLY REVIEWER HAS SEEN IT AND
EVERY CRITICAL AND IMPORTANT FINDING IS RESOLVED OR RECORDED AS DEFERRED.
```

**Read-only** is a trust boundary, not a performance note: the reviewer reads
anything, runs read-only checks, and writes nothing — not source, not git, not
run state. You stay the single writer.

No exceptions. The first names its addressee; the rest hold for anyone.

- **Never run a reviewer in the background — you, the agent in a herdr pane,
  where ending a turn *is* how you report done.** Do not set
  `run_in_background`, do not yield, and do not schedule a wakeup while one is
  out. A backgrounded reviewer parks you mid-turn, indistinguishable from a
  finished turn, and the run stalls until a human nudges the pane. Dispatch it
  blocking and read its verdict in the turn you dispatched it. That reason is
  role-specific, so there is exactly one role it does not bind: the **driver**,
  which backgrounds the panel and ends the turn because its harness re-invokes
  it on process exit — `skills/pipeline/SKILL.md` says so at its own loop. A
  split by role, not a preference. In a pane, the prohibition is yours.
- **Do not judge a change too small to review.** A one-line edit to a condition
  is the size this skill exists for. Dispatch a reviewer over it.
- **Do not count your own read as the review.** Re-reading your diff tells you
  it matches what you intended — the one thing never in doubt. Dispatch someone
  who does not know it.
- **Do not leave it for the pipeline's review phase.** That phase reads what you
  hand it, after later work is built on it. Dispatch here, while the change is
  one commit wide.
- **Do not close a finding by disagreeing with it.** When you will not fix one,
  quote it and write the reason in the report or handoff. An unrecorded
  decision reads downstream like an unread finding.
- **Do not repeat a verdict you have not read.** Open the file the reviewer
  names, or re-run the review when it named none. A reviewer that never came
  back has not said "clean".

## Announce

Say this out loud before dispatching anything:

```
Using drovr:code-review — dispatching read-only reviewers before calling this done.
```

## The procedure

> When a skill or briefing gives you a numbered checklist, create **one tracked item per step**
> using whatever task tool this harness exposes — `TodoWrite`, or `TaskCreate`/`TaskUpdate` —
> before you start step 1. Mark each in-progress when you start it and complete when its
> evidence is in hand. If the harness exposes no task tool, write the checklist to
> `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<run>/checklist.md` when inside a run, or `CHECKLIST.md` at the
> repo root otherwise, and tick items there. An untracked checklist decays with the context
> window; that decay is the exact failure drovr exists to fight.

Re-create those items for each change you review, not once for the session.

1. **Write down the change and the exact range** — the files, and `<base>..HEAD`.
   Get it wrong and the reviewer reports clean on nothing.
2. **Dispatch read-only reviewers, blocking, one per angle:** run
   `drovr code-review run <run> <task>` (`<base>` from `<task>-base.sha`, recorded
   before your first edit) — or, **inline** with no run,
   `drovr code-review run --base "$(git merge-base HEAD main)" <task>`. Nothing
   else, and never invent a run to get one.

   It spawns one reviewer per **configured** angle — `config.angles`, which
   defaults to correctness, security, error-handling, type-design — each writing
   `<task>-review-<angle>.json`, merged into `<task>-review.json`. **Read the
   config, not this page**, and cover any lens it omits yourself.

   Tell each reviewer to review as a skeptic, not the author; to say whether the
   tests exercise the behaviour, not just that they pass; to rate every finding
   **Critical, Important or nit** — what the Iron Law gates on — and say so when
   it found none; and to write them to a path you name, so step 3 has something
   to open. The lenses to cover:
   - **Spec compliance** — what was agreed, no more, no less?
   - **Correctness** — real bugs, unhandled cases, broken invariants.
   - **Verification** — do the claimed tests exist, and would they fail on a
     regression?
   - **Quality** — reuse, simplification, consistency with the code around it.
3. **Wait for every reviewer, then read what each wrote.** Open the findings
   file by path, then classify the round by how the panel exited:

   | Exit | What it means |
   |---|---|
   | 0 | clean — a real range was reviewed, nothing blocking |
   | 3 | blocking findings; go to step 5 |
   | 2 | timeout — reviewers are slow, not broken. Re-run the same command: it resumes the panel in flight |
   | 1 | error, or an empty `<base>..HEAD` it refused. Fix the range or the setup; never re-run blindly |
   | 137/143 | **your own harness killed it.** drovr produced no verdict at all, and none of the rows above describes the run. Re-run to resume, and record the round as **unclassifiable** — never as a timeout |

   A reviewer that returned no verdict is none of the five: re-dispatch rather
   than report its silence.

   **Only 0 is clean, and one clean round does not end the loop.** Stop at
   whichever of three comes first:
   - **Two consecutive clean rounds over an unchanged HEAD.** Any edit between
     them resets the count — the second round is evidence about the first only
     if it read the same code.
   - **A cap of six rounds**, which is *not* a clean ending: write up every
     round's verdict and everything still open (step 5), and finish on that
     record rather than on a verdict. Only rounds that delivered every
     configured angle count toward the cap — a missing angle is a Critical
     stand-in, so a round that lost a reviewer never measured the code.
   - **Two consecutive rounds that lost a dimension** — its own outcome,
     neither clean nor the cap: the panel is failing to deliver and further
     rounds are not measuring the code. Name the angles that never ran. Without
     this the loop cannot end at all, since such a round is never clean and
     never counts toward the cap.

   Three caveats the rule owes you. Two cleans make a false clean **less
   likely**, not unlikely, and prove nothing about convergence — in forge#88's
   own data two consecutive cleans preceded a `changes` round with seven
   findings. **Six is a starting number, revisable on evidence**, not a
   principled constant. And every word of this is prose nothing enforces — the
   shape of the *"re-run it"* that produced 47 re-arms over 14 hours.
4. **Check what the reviewer actually read — range *and* working tree.** The
   range must be the whole of `<base>..HEAD`, every file you touched, not a
   subset you picked; **and uncommitted work is in scope, not exempt** — drovr's
   panel reviews the diff *plus the current working tree*. A verdict covers what
   is on disk only if the reviewer saw both. Clean on an empty range, a subset,
   or a tree with unreviewed edits in it is about a change nobody read.
5. **Resolve every Critical and Important finding, or record the deferral with
   `drovr code-review defer`.** Per finding: quote it, then name the edit
   answering it by file — or, if you are not making it, run

   ```
   drovr code-review defer <RUN> <TASK> --file <path> [--line <n>] \
     --severity <critical|important|nit> --summary "<the finding>" \
     --reason "<why it is not being fixed>"
   ```

   A deferral written only in prose is one the next round cannot read, so it
   re-raises the finding you already ruled on. The command appends to a
   per-task log every later seed carries; prose does not.
6. **Re-run the checks after your last review-driven edit, then say it is
   done.** The fixes are new, unverified code: run the tests. When the change is
   not code and has no suite, name what you re-read instead and why it covers the
   edits — written down, never assumed. Report the findings, the edits and the
   deferrals; inside a drovr phase this also gates `drovr phase done`. **Done is
   step 3's termination rule met, not the first exit 0** — say which of the
   three ended it, and on the cap or a lost dimension say plainly that the loop
   ended on a record rather than on a clean verdict.

## Requirements

The middle column is what the claim takes; the right is what gets accepted
instead.

| The claim | Required evidence | NOT sufficient |
|---|---|---|
| *"This change has been reviewed"* | A read-only reviewer dispatched over this change in the foreground, returned in this turn, and the range you handed it, written down | Your own re-read · a reviewer launched and not waited for · a review of the tree before your last edit |
| *"The reviewer found nothing"* | The findings file it wrote, opened by path and read by you — or the review re-run by you when it wrote none — **and** what it read shown to be the whole of `<base>..HEAD` **plus your working tree** | Its summary, however much output it pastes · exit 1 or 2 · a subset of your files · uncommitted edits nobody looked at · a verdict that never arrived |
| *"Every Critical and Important finding is resolved"* | Each quoted, the edit answering it named by file, and step 6's checks re-run after the last edit | A count · agreeing with one in prose · fixing the Criticals and leaving the Importants |
| *"That finding does not apply here"* | The finding quoted, and the reason written where the next agent reads it | Deciding it in your head · *"out of scope"* with no scope named · silence, which downstream reads as resolved |

## Red flags — STOP

Some are thoughts, some are things you have just written. Either way you are at
the line.

- *"They are going to read it line by line anyway."* · *"The lead said just
  send it."* · *"It is a two-line change."* · *"I already reviewed it myself."*
  · *"The pipeline's review phase will catch it."* — each opens a row in
  *Rationalizations*, verbatim. Go do the thing in its row.
- *You are about to launch a reviewer in the background and keep working.* →
  Dispatch it blocking. No version of that ends with you reading its verdict
  this turn.
- *A reviewer has not come back and you are writing the report.* → Block on it.
  Silence is not a pass; a parked reviewer is not a finished one.
- *The panel came back clean in seconds on a large diff.* → Check what it read.
  Clean and empty look identical from here.
- **Anything that treats the change as finished** — any wording at all, and
  also committing, opening a PR, or starting the next task — while a reviewer is
  unread, unreturned, or holding an unresolved Critical or Important finding. If
  you cannot name the reviewer and point at what it wrote, change what you
  dispatched, not how you word it.

## Rationalizations

The right column is an instruction, not an argument. Do the thing in it.

| The thought | Do this instead |
|---|---|
| *"They are going to read it line by line anyway."* | Dispatch the reviewer first, then send it. Two different reads: theirs is for fit, the review's is for correctness, and one does not make the other redundant — reading a document aloud catches prose gaps, not retry semantics. |
| *"The lead said just send it."* | Send it after the review, and tell them the call moves. That is a scheduling reflex, not anyone weighing the technical risk — the calendar is theirs, the correctness yours. |
| *"It is a two-line change."* | Dispatch a reviewer over the two lines. Size is not a risk measure, and the risk you estimate in order to skip the review is what it would have told you. |
| *"I already reviewed it myself."* | Dispatch one that did not write it. Your read confirms the diff matches your intent; the defects worth catching are in what you did not think of. |
| *"The pipeline's review phase will catch it."* | Dispatch here, now. That phase reads what you hand it, after later tasks built on it; a finding costs more at every step it survives. |
| *"The reviewer came back with no findings."* | Open the file it named, and check it read your whole change, working tree included. An empty range comes back clean from every angle at once. |

## Worked example

One read away, in `skills/code-review/worked-example.md`: a 320-line spec, a
client call in 19 minutes, a $45,000 sign-off and a lead writing *"just send
it"* — the rationalization refused, the panel run, two Importants found, the
call moved 22 minutes. Worth reading once; the rules above do not depend on it.

## Cross-refs

- `drovr:verification-before-completion` — REQUIRED before you repeat a
  verdict: a reviewer's report is a claim, not evidence.
- `drovr:systematic-debugging` — REQUIRED when a finding is a bug: it is a
  report, not a diagnosis. Reproduce before you fix.
- `drovr:tdd` — REQUIRED when a finding needs new behaviour: the fix is new code
  and gets a failing test.
- `drovr:handoff` — REQUIRED at a phase boundary: deferred findings travel in the
  handoff or not at all.
- `drovr:pipeline` — the driver's side of both split rules: it backgrounds the
  panel, and it runs step 3's termination rule from the loop's end.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Host-package helpers for ./deploy. Sourced, never executed: sourcing is what
# lets ../tests/system-packages.sh drive these against a temp tree instead of
# /etc. Nothing here has an effect at source time, and every path is an
# argument -- no function reaches for a location of its own.
#
# SUDO is the privilege seam, and it is `${SUDO-sudo}`, not `${SUDO:-sudo}`:
# the tests set it to the empty string to mean "write as me", which the :-
# form would quietly turn back into sudo.

# Packages wanted on this host: the shared ./packages plus the optional
# per-host ./packages.<host>, which is how a box gets something the others
# have no business installing (steam on shiori and not on headless fujiwara).
#
# The format is one package per line with # comments, and the split is on any
# whitespace rather than per line: a two-names-on-one-line slip then fails as
# two packages pacman reports missing, instead of one concatenated name that
# silently never installs. Deduped, order preserved -- a name in both lists
# reaches pacman once, so the "installing missing" line stays readable.
#
# A missing per-host file is the normal case, not an error. The shared list's
# existence is ./deploy's check, because only deploy knows it is fatal there.
pacman_wants() { # pacman_wants <dir> <host>
  local dir=$1 host=$2 f
  for f in "$dir/packages" "$dir/packages.$host"; do
    # Quoted, so a host name containing a glob character is looked up
    # literally rather than expanded against the directory.
    [ -e "$f" ] || continue
    sed 's/#.*//' -- "$f"
  done | tr -s '[:space:]' '\n' | sed '/^$/d' | awk '!seen[$0]++'
}

# Append <line> to <conf> unless it is already there, and say so when it does.
# The one place this repo writes to a pacman-owned file: /etc/pacman.conf is a
# pacman backup file, so it cannot live under ./etc the way our override files
# do, and enabling a repo needs exactly one line in it. Everything that line
# pulls in stays in the repo, under ./etc/pacman.d/conf.d/.
#
#   • -qxF: whole line, fixed string. The stock pacman.conf ships commented
#     example Include lines, and a substring match would read one as "already
#     enabled" and never enable anything.
#   • the leading \n: an /etc file edited by hand may end without a newline,
#     and a blind append would glue the Include onto that last line. A blank
#     line in pacman.conf is inert.
#   • the echo: deploy's output is where a reader learns a root-owned file
#     outside this repo was edited. Silence on the no-op run is the point.
pacman_ensure_include() { # pacman_ensure_include <conf> <line>
  local conf=$1 line=$2
  grep -qxF -- "$line" "$conf" 2>/dev/null && return 0
  printf '\n%s\n' "$line" | ${SUDO-sudo} tee -a -- "$conf" >/dev/null
  echo "enabled in ${conf}: ${line}"
}

# Does <dbdir> hold a sync db for <repo>? Enabling a repo does not fetch one,
# and `pacman -S` against a repo with no db answers "target not found" -- which
# reads as a bad package name rather than as "you never synced". deploy checks
# this so it can say the real thing instead. It deliberately does not fix it:
# `pacman -Sy` without the -u is the partial-upgrade footgun deploy avoids
# everywhere else, so the cure is a human running `pacman -Syu`.
pacman_repo_synced() { # pacman_repo_synced <dbdir> <repo>
  [ -e "$1/$2.db" ]
}

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Enable thermald where it is installed, and nowhere else.
#
# The split of labour with ./packages.<host>: that list decides WHICH hosts want
# thermald (today only ./packages.shiori), and ./deploy's pacman step installs
# it. This script does the one thing a package list cannot express -- `pacman -S`
# puts a unit on disk, it does not start it or wire it into a target, and
# install-base.sh's `systemctl enable` line runs once inside the chroot of a
# fresh install, so it only ever reaches the NEXT new host. That gap is how
# fprintd stayed uninstalled for months; a daemon nobody enabled is the same gap
# with the same shape.
#
# So the gate here is "is thermald installed", not the CPU vendor. Deliberately:
# a vendor check here would be a second, independent answer to a question the
# per-host list already answers, and the two would drift. thermald is Intel-only
# -- it steers the ACPI DPTF devices (int3400/int3403) and the
# processor_thermal_device RAPL knobs, and exits on anything else -- but that is
# an argument about which list it belongs in, which is settled in the list.
#
# WHY thermald AT ALL: it is the Framework/Intel recommendation, not a hunch.
# ArchWiki's Framework Laptop 13 page ("Lowering fan noise") names it for the
# Intel version specifically; both distributions Framework certifies the Laptop
# 13 Pro against -- Ubuntu 26.04 LTS and Fedora 44 -- ship it by default on
# Intel; and Phoronix ran its Panther Lake performance-profile numbers with
# thermald applied. shiori is a Framework Laptop 13 Pro (Core Ultra X7 358H,
# Panther Lake) and has the int3400/int3403 devices thermald steers.
#
# It coexists with power-profiles-daemon rather than replacing it: ppd sets the
# EPP and the ACPI platform_profile, thermald manages the passive trip points and
# fan response underneath. That pairing is what Fedora and Ubuntu both ship.
#
# Seams, for ../tests/thermald-setup.sh: pacman, sudo and systemctl are resolved
# through PATH, so the harness stubs them and no case needs a real package, a
# real unit, or root.
set -euo pipefail

# The host asked for thermald by listing it, or it did not. Nothing to do is the
# normal case on three of four hosts, and it has to be silent -- a deploy step
# that narrates its own no-op on every run trains people to skim the output.
if ! pacman -Qq thermald >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  exit 0
fi

# is-enabled/is-active are unprivileged where `enable --now` is not, so asking
# first is what keeps a converged host at zero sudo prompts. ./deploy runs on
# every `mise run system:deploy`; a step that escalated unconditionally would
# turn the password prompt into background noise.
#
# Both halves matter. Enabled-but-stopped is a live host where someone ran
# `systemctl stop`; active-but-disabled is one that loses the daemon at the next
# reboot. Either way `enable --now` is the same idempotent fix.
if [ "$(systemctl is-enabled thermald.service 2>/dev/null)" != enabled ] ||
  [ "$(systemctl is-active thermald.service 2>/dev/null)" != active ]; then
  echo "system/thermald-setup: enabling thermald.service"
  sudo systemctl enable --now thermald.service
fi

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Cases for system/thermald-setup, the enable-half of the thermald story that
# system/deploy runs right after its package convergence. They drive the real
# script with stub pacman/sudo/systemctl on PATH, so no case needs the package,
# the unit, root, or an Intel host, and none of them can touch this machine.
#
# What is actually being protected here, in two halves:
#
#   The gate. Which hosts want thermald is decided by ./packages.<host>, so this
#   script must do nothing whatsoever on a host that did not list it. A gate that
#   leaked would enable a unit that is not installed -- on utsuho and fujiwara
#   that is a failure on every boot, which is exactly the outcome keeping
#   thermald out of the shared list was for.
#
#   The silence. A converged host must escalate zero times. system/deploy runs on
#   every `mise run system:deploy`, and a step that sudo'd unconditionally would
#   turn the password prompt into background noise -- so "no sudo at all on the
#   no-op path" is a real assertion, not a tidiness one.
#
#   ./tests/thermald-setup.sh                 # tests system/thermald-setup
#   ./tests/thermald-setup.sh /path/to/script # tests one you already have
set -u

SCRIPT="${1:-$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../system" && pwd)/thermald-setup}"
[ -x "$SCRIPT" ] || { echo "not executable: $SCRIPT" >&2; exit 1; }
echo "testing $SCRIPT"

D=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$D"' EXIT
fails=0; n=0

# --- stubs -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Each records its argv in $D/calls and answers from a STUB_* variable, so a case
# reads as "what the host looks like" rather than as a script of mocks.
mkdir -p "$D/bin"

cat > "$D/bin/pacman" <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "pacman $*" >> "$CALLS"
case "$1" in
-Qq) exit "${STUB_INSTALLED:-1}" ;;   # 0 = thermald installed on this host
esac
exit 0
EOF

# Not `exec "$@"` blindly: recording the sudo itself is what lets a case assert
# that the converged path never escalates at all.
cat > "$D/bin/sudo" <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "sudo $*" >> "$CALLS"
exec "$@"
EOF

cat > "$D/bin/systemctl" <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "systemctl $*" >> "$CALLS"
case "$1" in
is-enabled) echo "${STUB_ENABLED:-disabled}"; [ "${STUB_ENABLED:-disabled}" = enabled ] ;;
is-active)  echo "${STUB_ACTIVE:-inactive}";  [ "${STUB_ACTIVE:-inactive}" = active ] ;;
enable)     exit "${STUB_ENABLE_RC:-0}" ;;
esac
exit 0
EOF

chmod +x "$D/bin"/*

# --- runner ------------------------------------------------------------------
# want_rc, then a list of "+needle" (must appear in the call log) and "-needle"
# (must not). Env for the case comes in as leading VAR=value arguments, and
# `want_out` is matched against combined stdout+stderr when it is not empty.
run_case() { # desc want_rc [VAR=val ...] -- [+/-needle ...]
  local desc=$1 want_rc=$2; shift 2
  local env=() rc out
  while [ $# -gt 0 ] && [ "$1" != -- ]; do env+=("$1"); shift; done
  [ $# -gt 0 ] && shift

  n=$((n + 1))
  : > "$D/calls"
  out=$(env PATH="$D/bin:$PATH" CALLS="$D/calls" "${env[@]}" "$SCRIPT" 2>&1)
  rc=$?

  local bad=() needle
  [ "$rc" = "$want_rc" ] || bad+=("exit $rc, wanted $want_rc")
  for needle in "$@"; do
    case "$needle" in
    out:) [ -z "$out" ] || bad+=("wanted no output, got: $out") ;;
    +*) grep -qF -- "${needle#+}" "$D/calls" || bad+=("missing call: ${needle#+}") ;;
    -*) grep -qF -- "${needle#-}" "$D/calls" && bad+=("unwanted call: ${needle#-}") ;;
    esac
  done

  if [ ${#bad[@]} -eq 0 ]; then
    echo "ok   $desc"
  else
    fails=$((fails + 1))
    echo "FAIL $desc"
    printf '       %s\n' "${bad[@]}"
    printf '       calls: %s\n' "$(tr '\n' '; ' < "$D/calls")"
    [ -n "$out" ] && printf '       output: %s\n' "$out"
  fi
}

# --- the gate ----------------------------------------------------------------
# The host never listed thermald. Nothing may happen -- and in particular
# `systemctl` must not be reached at all, because the only thing this script
# could do with an uninstalled unit is enable a failure.
run_case "package absent: does nothing" 0 STUB_INSTALLED=1 -- \
  -"systemctl" -"sudo" +"pacman -Qq thermald"

# ...and says nothing either. Three of four hosts take this path on every single
# deploy; narrating a no-op there is how output stops being read.
run_case "package absent: says nothing" 0 STUB_INSTALLED=1 -- out:

# --- the listed host ---------------------------------------------------------
# The run that just installed it: ./deploy's pacman step put the unit on disk,
# and this is the step that makes it actually run, without a reboot.
run_case "listed, unit untouched: enables and starts" 0 \
  STUB_INSTALLED=0 STUB_ENABLED=disabled STUB_ACTIVE=inactive -- \
  +"systemctl enable --now thermald.service" +"sudo"

# The prompt-free no-op, and the reason the two is-* checks exist at all. If this
# case ever logs a sudo, every deploy starts asking for a password to do nothing.
run_case "converged: no escalation at all" 0 \
  STUB_INSTALLED=0 STUB_ENABLED=enabled STUB_ACTIVE=active -- \
  -"sudo" +"systemctl is-enabled thermald.service"

# Both halves of the check earn their keep, and they fail differently: enabled-
# but-stopped is a live host where someone ran `systemctl stop`, active-but-
# disabled is one that silently loses the daemon at the next reboot.
run_case "enabled but stopped: re-enables" 0 \
  STUB_INSTALLED=0 STUB_ENABLED=enabled STUB_ACTIVE=inactive -- \
  +"systemctl enable --now thermald.service"
run_case "running but disabled: re-enables" 0 \
  STUB_INSTALLED=0 STUB_ENABLED=disabled STUB_ACTIVE=active -- \
  +"systemctl enable --now thermald.service"

# A unit in no state systemd has a word for (masked, not-found, a systemd too old
# to answer) is not "converged" -- it must take the enable path, not the silent
# one. This is what would break if the checks were ever loosened to "not
# disabled".
run_case "unknown unit state: still tries to enable" 0 \
  STUB_INSTALLED=0 STUB_ENABLED=masked STUB_ACTIVE=failed -- \
  +"systemctl enable --now thermald.service"

# --- failure -----------------------------------------------------------------
# A failed enable has to leave as a non-zero status: that is what makes
# system/deploy's `|| echo ... continuing` print, rather than the deploy
# reporting success over a daemon that never started.
run_case "enable failure is reported" 1 \
  STUB_INSTALLED=0 STUB_ENABLED=disabled STUB_ACTIVE=inactive STUB_ENABLE_RC=1 -- \
  +"systemctl enable --now thermald.service"

echo
if [ "$fails" -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "all $n cases passed"
else
  echo "$fails of $n cases FAILED"
fi
exit $((fails > 0))

Panther Lake performance-profile numbers with it applied. It sits under ppd
rather than replacing it -- ppd owns the EPP and the ACPI platform_profile,
thermald the passive trip points and the fan response.

It goes in ./packages.shiori, not the shared list, because it is Intel-only: on
utsuho and fujiwara it would be a unit that fails on every boot, which is the one
way a wrongly-placed package is not merely inert.

Installing it does not start it, and no package list can say "and run it".
install-base.sh's `systemctl enable` line runs once inside the chroot of a fresh
install, so it only ever reaches the NEXT new host -- the same gap that kept
fprintd uninstalled for months, in the same shape. So ./deploy runs
./thermald-setup right after convergence. Its gate is "is thermald installed",
not a CPU check: a vendor test there would be a second, independent answer to the
question ./packages.<host> already answers, and the two would drift.

Also home.nix, shiori only: framework-tool. Framework exposes no
charge_control_end_threshold under /sys, so `framework_tool --charge-limit` is
the only way to set one. It wants sudo but not a system unit, so by
system/packages' own rule it is a user package.

Not done, deliberately: the acpi_osi="!Windows 2020" and nvme.noacpi=1 kernel
parameters the wiki lists for Intel Frameworks. Both fix 11th/12th-gen faults --
an s2idle regression and an NVMe that will not wake. This box suspends and
resumes cleanly, and neither is a parameter to carry on faith.

tests/thermald-setup.sh drives the real script with stub pacman/sudo/systemctl,
asserting the two things that would hurt: a host that never listed thermald does
nothing at all (and says nothing), and a converged host escalates zero times.
Both mutations -- dropping the installed check, dropping the already-enabled
check -- fail it.

`tests/system-packages.sh` case 16 copies the host's real /etc/pacman.conf,
appends a glob Include pointing at a temp copy of the repo's drop-in, and
asserted that pacman then registers multilib exactly once.

appended and twice after, and the case fails with want 1, got 2. It has been

when the mechanism it justifies started working.

Fixed by measuring the delta rather than the total: count multilib registrations
in the copy, append the Include, count again, and assert the difference is 1.
That states what the design actually rests on -- one glob Include matching the
repo's drop-in adds one multilib repo -- and states it identically on a fresh
host and a converged one.

A narrower fix that stripped the conf.d Include line out of the copy would have
worked here and still broken on a host whose stock [multilib] section is simply
uncommented, which registers multilib without any Include at all. The delta does
not care how the host got there.

copied in as an empty file the case fails with a delta of 0, so it still has
teeth; with the conf.d Include filtered out of the copy, simulating a host that
